[1] AMLR, Article 11(1): Compliance functions
1. Obliged entities shall appoint one member of the management body in its management function who shall be responsible for ensuring compliance with this Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2023/1113 and any administrative act issued by any supervisor (‘compliance manager’).
The compliance manager shall ensure that the obliged entity’s internal policies, procedures and controls are consistent with the obliged entity’s risk exposure and that they are implemented. The compliance manager shall also ensure that sufficient human and material resources are allocated to that end. The compliance manager shall be responsible for receiving information on significant or material weaknesses in such policies, procedures and controls.
Where the management body in its management function is a body collectively responsible for its decisions, the compliance manager shall be responsible for assisting and advising it and for preparing the decisions referred to in this Article.

[2] AMLR, Article 11(6): Compliance functions
6. The compliance manager shall regularly report on the implementation of the obliged entity’s internal policies, procedures and controls to the management body. In particular, the compliance manager shall submit once a year, or, where appropriate, more frequently, to the management body a report on the implementation of the obliged entity’s internal policies, procedures and controls drawn up by the compliance officer, and shall keep that body informed of the outcome of any reviews. The compliance manager shall take the necessary actions to remedy in a timely manner any deficiencies identified.

[3] AMLR, Article 16(2): Group-wide requirements
2. Compliance functions shall be established at the level of the group. Those functions shall include a compliance manager at the level of the group and, where justified by the activities carried out at group level, a compliance officer. The decision on the extent of the compliance functions shall be documented.
The compliance manager referred to in the first subparagraph shall regularly report to the management body in its management function of the parent undertaking on the implementation of the group-wide policies, procedures and controls. At a minimum, the compliance manager shall submit once a year a report on the implementation of the obliged entity’s internal policies, procedures and controls and shall take the necessary actions to remedy in a timely manner any deficiencies identified. Where the management body in its management function is a body collectively responsible for its decisions, the compliance manager shall assist and advise it, and shall prepare the decisions necessary for the implementation of this Article.

In our company, the management team makes decisions collectively—such as approving new product launches or major changes to our risk policies. How do we ensure that the compliance manager is effectively involved in these decisions, especially when there’s a material risk weakness identified in our internal controls during a product launch review?

Where the management body in its management function is a body collectively responsible for its decisions, the compliance manager shall assist and advise it and shall prepare the decisions referred to in this Article [AMLR, Article 11(1)]. The compliance manager shall be responsible for receiving information on significant or material weaknesses in such policies, procedures and controls [AMLR, Article 11(1)]. In the case of a material risk weakness identified during a product launch review, the compliance manager must promptly inform the management body and assist in preparing decisions to address the deficiency [AMLR, Article 11(1)]. The compliance manager shall also regularly report on the implementation of internal policies, procedures and controls to the management body, including the outcome of any reviews [AMLR, Article 11(6)]. This ensures that material risks are properly assessed and that decisions are informed by compliance oversight [AMLR, Article 11(6)].

How should we prepare for the upcoming submission of draft technical standards to the Commission, and what steps should our compliance team take to ensure we are aligned with the requirements for cooperation between competent authorities under the current timeline?

To prepare for the upcoming submission of draft technical standards to the Commission, the compliance team should first identify the relevant regulatory frameworks, such as MiCA, PSD2, and DORA, which mandate the development of draft regulatory or implementing technical standards for cooperation between competent authorities [MiCA, Article 95(10)]; [PSD2, Article 28(5)]; [DORA, Article 41]. The team must ensure alignment with specific requirements, including the specification of information to be exchanged, standard forms, templates, and procedures for notification and cooperation [MiCA, Article 95(11)]; [PSD2, Article 28(5)]; [DORA, Article 41]. They should coordinate closely with ESMA, EBA, or relevant authorities to develop consistent and efficient cooperation frameworks, particularly in defining common terminology and standardized notification templates [PSD2, Article 28(5)]; [DORA, Article 41]. Finally, the compliance team must adhere to the submission deadlines—such as 30 June 2024 for MiCA and PSD2, and 17 July 2024 for DORA—and ensure that the draft standards are reviewed and approved in accordance with the Commission’s adoption procedures under Regulation (EU) No 1095/2010 or related regulations [MiCA, Article 95(11)]; [PSD2, Article 28(5)]; [DORA, Article 41].

If a customer repeatedly submits the same data access request under the GDPR, and we receive a notice from a supervisory authority stating that the request is manifestly unfounded or excessive, what steps should we take to ensure we are not unfairly burdened by processing such requests, and how can we demonstrate that the request meets the threshold for being considered manifestly excessive?

If a customer repeatedly submits the same data access request, the controller may charge a reasonable fee based on administrative costs or refuse to act on the request, provided the request is manifestly unfounded or excessive, particularly due to its repetitive character [GDPR, Article 12(5)]. The controller bears the burden of demonstrating that the request is manifestly unfounded or excessive [GDPR, Article 12(5)]. To demonstrate that the request meets the threshold for being considered manifestly excessive, the controller must show that the request is repetitive, lacks legitimate purpose, and does not contribute to the data subject’s right to access, thereby justifying administrative cost limitations [GDPR, Article 12(5)]. The supervisory authority may also assess such requests for manifest unfoundedness, and the controller must provide evidence of repetition and lack of substance to support the determination [GDPR, Article 12(5)].

If a staff member in our finance department is authorized to access customer data to perform routine financial reporting, and they occasionally share that data with a third-party vendor for compliance purposes without explicit written instructions from our legal team, does that constitute a breach of the security requirements under this rule?

No, this does not constitute a breach of the security requirements under the rule, as the GDPR Article 32(4) requires only that natural persons acting under the authority of the controller or processor must not process personal data except on instructions from the controller, unless required by Union or Member State law. The staff member’s access to customer data is permitted under routine financial reporting, which is a legitimate business function, and the sharing with a third-party vendor for compliance purposes, without explicit written instructions from the legal team, may not meet the requirement of explicit instructions unless such sharing is specifically authorized. However, the absence of explicit written instructions from the legal team may indicate a failure to ensure compliance with data protection principles, particularly under the requirement of proper authorization and oversight. [GDPR, Article 32(4)]

If a fintech firm in our country receives a penalty for non-compliance with a rule related to customer authentication, can we expect the competent authority to publicly disclose the penalty, and under what conditions would such disclosure be prevented?

Yes, the competent authority may publicly disclose the penalty if it is imposed for an infringement of a rule related to customer authentication, provided that such disclosure would not seriously jeopardise financial stability or cause disproportionate damage to the parties involved [PSD2, Article 103]. Disclosure would be prevented if the public release of the penalty would seriously jeopardise financial markets or cause disproportionate damage to the parties involved [PSD2, Article 103]. This condition aligns with the principle of proportionality and protection of sensitive information in financial regulation.

If a critical ICT third-party service provider receives recommendations from the Lead Overseer to improve their cybersecurity measures, and the provider decides not to implement those recommendations, what specific information must they provide to the Lead Overseer, and what obligations do the financial entities have in response to this situation?

The critical ICT third-party service provider must either notify the Lead Overseer of their intention to follow the recommendations or provide a reasoned explanation for not following them, within 60 calendar days of receiving the recommendations [DORA, Article 42(1)]. The Lead Overseer shall immediately transmit this information to the competent authorities of the financial entities concerned [DORA, Article 42(1)]. In response, the financial entities are obligated to consider the situation and may, in certain circumstances, require the termination of contractual arrangements with the provider if the non-compliance poses a significant risk to financial stability [DORA, Article 39(7)].

The certification program should establish data protection certification mechanisms and seals or marks approved under GDPR, Article 42(2), to demonstrate appropriate safeguards for third-party service providers, particularly when data transfers occur to third countries or international organisations [GDPR, Article 42(2)]. The program may use an approved certification mechanism as an element to demonstrate compliance with the data protection by design and by default principles under GDPR, Article 25, including data minimisation and default processing limits [GDPR, Article 25]. When we identify a customer who is the subject of an ongoing investigation by a law enforcement body, and we receive a request to share personal data with a third party for risk assessment purposes, how should we ensure that we correctly distinguish between the stage of an investigation and a final conviction, especially when the customer has not yet been formally charged?

When identifying a customer who is the subject of an ongoing investigation by a law enforcement body, obliged entities must ensure that they distinguish between allegations, investigations, proceedings, and convictions, taking into account the fundamental right to a fair trial, the right of defence and the presumption of innocence [AMLR, Article 76(3)]. Since the customer has not yet been formally charged, the processing of personal data remains at the stage of an investigation, not a conviction, and thus falls under the category of allegations or investigations rather than proceedings or convictions [AMLR, Article 76(3)]. This distinction is essential to ensure compliance with the fundamental rights enshrined in the legal framework, particularly where personal data are processed in relation to money laundering, its predicate offences or terrorist financing [AMLR, Article 76(3)]. The entity must apply appropriate procedures to maintain such distinctions, especially when sharing personal data with a third party for risk assessment purposes, to avoid treating an ongoing investigation as a final conviction [AMLR, Article 76(3)].
